1. **Chart type**  
   Grouped horizontal bar chart (progress-bar style bars).

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **small multiples / column grouping** by surname outcome category: “Took spouse’s name,” “Kept name,” and “Hyphenated.”
   - Within each column, bars are arranged by **race/ethnicity group**.
   - Not stacked; each bar is shown separately against a common background track.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Bride surname outcome (“Took spouse’s name”, “Kept name”, “Hyphenated”) | Categorical/nominal | Column grouping / panel heading |
| Race/ethnicity (“White”, “Black”, “Hispanic”) | Categorical/nominal | Row position; text labels at left |
| Percentage | Quantitative | Bar length (horizontal extent); numeric labels inside/next to bars |

comments.raw_comment:
What I notice: 
- A comparative bar chart is presented
- Most brides take their spouse’s last name, but the percentage varies by race.
- White brides do this the most (86%), while Hispanic brides do it the least (60%).
- Black brides are the most likely to hyphenate their names (16%).
What I wonder: 
- Why do Hispanic brides keep their last name more often?
- How do culture and religion influence these choices?
- Would the trend be different in same-sex marriages?
How this relates to me and my community: 
Being part of a Jewish community, taking a spouse’s last name is not just a tradition but an expectation. In many Jewish marriages, women adopt their husband’s surname as part of religious and cultural norms. However, hyphenating last names is pretty common in my community, often to honor both family names and maintain a connection to one’s heritage. However, keeping a maiden name entirely is unheard of, as it may be seen as breaking from tradition.
Catchy headline: "Tying the Knot, Changing the Name?"

I am speculating it has something to do with culture and tradition, as mentioned previously, the majority of women take their husband's last name because that is what has usually been done in Western Society. I know that Hispanic surnames are really important meaning - wise, especially in such family-centric cultures, so the carrying on of the familial history through the name could be one contributor of Hispanic women keeping their own name. I would assume the same is true for Black women who want to preserve their family history. 

This relates to me and my community because I will likely get married, and am part of the new generation that will marry. As a non-white person of mixed race, I've definitely thought about hyphenating my own name. I think this trend will increase as more people have interracial marriages.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that American women change their names to varying degrees: 86% of White brides, 73% of Black brides, 60% of Hispanic brides take their spouse's name. Interestingly, Black brides were most likely to hyphenate their names (16%) and Hispanic brides were more likely to keep their name (30%).

I wonder why such a large number of White brides take their spouse's name. Perhaps tradition dictates this trend. Furthermore, since Hispanic individuals often have more than one middle name, perhaps it is related to the bride's not changing their name. I wonder if fewer women will take their spouse's name in the future, considering how difficult it can be to change legal documents.

This relates to me and my community because my generation will be getting married in the next 15 years. As more couples are of mixed race, these statistics may change. I imagine that the number of brides that take their spouse's names will decrease across all races.

"Getting Hitched: Ditching the Name"

comments.raw_comment:
Major Racial differences between last names	

In the website of brides changing their last names, we have noticed similar and different things. The graph is separated into how likely the bride change their last name based on race. The graph shows that white people choose to take the spouse's last name more commonly than Hispanics and black people do. While Hispanics are more likely to keep their last name than both black and white people are. Interestingly, white and Hispanic peoples data add up to 99% while black people’s data add up to 98%. Wondering where the missing percentages are going. We are also left wondering why it’s only those three races and not more. It might show others why some races are most likely to change their last name or keep it. We believe that this information has little impact on ourselves or our community. In conclusion,  we are a little surprised that the difference in brides' likelihood to give up their maiden name varies so much by race.

comments.raw_comment: There are a few trends I notice in the data presented, and I’m interested to know the reasons behind them. Firstly, the demographic most likely to take their husbands names are white brides, while black and hispanic brides are increasingly less likely to take their husband’s names. Black brides were by far the most likely to hyphenate their names, while Hispanic brides were the most likely to keep their maiden names. Of the white brides that did not take their husbands’ names the majority kept their maiden name, rather than hyphenate. I could speculate this to reflect different cultural norms around marriage. Particularly, you could see the significant minority of white brides keeping their maiden names as representing the population of progressive educated professional white women and the 90% who don’t as those who follow more traditional and Christian social moores, which is a division I’ve noticed in my life and communities.

I think those changes would make the results more representative of the women of the United States. This relates to me because my mom did not change her last name and it is interesting to see how much of a minority her choice was. A possible headline would be "To change your name or to keep your name"

comments.raw_comment: This graph depicts the percentage of brides changing their last name, either taking their spouse's name, keeping their name, or hyphenating it. The percentages vary based on race. I notice that most women of all races take their spouse's last names. I think this is simply because of tradition. Although a fairly large percentage of Hispanic women kept their last name, this may suggest that this tradition of taking your spouse's last name is not very important to Hispanic culture. I wonder if their are other gender traditions that Hispanic culture does not follow. I notice that out of all women who hyphenate their last name, Black women make up the majority, even though it is only 16 percent. I wonder if as time passes, and as a society progress, fewer women will take their spouse's name. I additionally wonder if white women will be the last to completely switch, if there ever is a complete switch. This affects me and my community as since I am a girl, if I get married, I will have to make the choice on what my last name will be. "To Keep or to Change?"

 However, out of everyone in the survey,Hispanic women were the  most likely to keep their last name with thirty percent of them keeping their name. I'm curious why they didn't broaden this survey to include more cultures, which would provide more information if keeping one last name is a cultural phenomena. This is relevant to my community because all of the married women I know have taken their spouses' names, and when I get married, I intend to do the same.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph shows the results from a survey that asked 2,740 married women in opposite-sex marriages what they do with their last names after marriage. The researchers separated these women into three categories based on their races (White, Black, and Hispanic). It is clear from this graph that the overwhelming majority of women take their spouse's name throughout all three races. However, out of all the races surveyed, Hispanic women were most likely to keep their last name as 30% of them chose to keep it compared to Black women (9%) and White (10%). While this graph only surveyed a tiny percentage of America's 332 million-person population, I think that Hispanic women's commitment to keeping their last name shows the pride that they have in maintaining their heritage, especially as a race that is so often discriminated against. Black women show similar respect for their heritage as 16% of Black women hyphenated their last names compared to 3% of White women and 9% of Hispanic women. This is interesting because I feel like I have never heard a hyphenated last name. I wonder how this graph would change if more people and races were included. For example, Asian women were left out of this graph as mentioned in the commentary. This relates to me because I am a young woman who hopes to get married one day, and eventually, will have to decide what to do with my last name. 
"Name Norms after Marriage"

comments.raw_comment:
The graph depicts the percentage of brides, based on their race, and their decision to change their name last after matrimony. For example, this graph shows that statistically, the majority of white brides, end up taking their spouse’s last name (86%). While a majority of Hispanic brides still take their spouse’s last name (60%), Hispanic brides are the most likely to keep their maiden names at 30% compared to white brides (10%) and Black brides (9%). What I wonder is why this survey was so limited. I understand this was a voluntary survey and only 2,740 American brides responded. Even though it was conducted by the Pew Research Center, a reliable source, it does not accurately represent women across America 68.45 million married women across America. Plus, this graph only pertains to same-sex couples and does not include Asian or Indigenous people. I wonder how much this graph would fluctuate if more people responded and more groups were represented. This relates to my community because as a young woman surrounded by other young women, if we choose to get married, we all have to one day decide the fate of our last names. More and more women feel less pressure to have to change their name to please their husbands and decaying, misogynistic societal standards. It will be interesting to see who leaves their last name, who keeps their last name, and who hyphenates.  

“Married Women: Who Will Have to Change Their Drivers License?”

comments.raw_comment:
This chart notes the percentage of women changing their last name in marriage across various racial groups.  White women are the most likely to change their last name to that of their husband's. Black women are most likely to hyphenate their last names, and Hispanic women are extremely likely to keep their last name altogether. 
I wonder why Hispanic women keep their name the most among the racial groups polled for the graph. While only 1 in 10 black or white women keep their name, around 1 in 3 Hispanic women do, which is a huge leap. Maybe it's for a cultural reason? I think that Hispanic families tend to be more close-knit, and many Hispanic people live in intergenerational households. It could be for this reason that Hispanic women want to keep this connection to their family and not take their husbands name.
More and more women are choosing to not take the traditional route of taking the husband's last name. It's interesting to see how this trend is occurring among various groups, especially since there are many women in my life.
HEADLINE: I Do or Don't: Say Yes to the Name

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, it is depicting the percentage of bridges who either took their spouse’s last name, kept their last name, or hyphenated the names for three different ethnicities/races (white, black, and hispanic). Additionally, I noticed that hispanic brides have the highest percentage of keeping their name with a percentage of 30% whereas white and black brides were less likely to keep their names. Also, black brides had the highest percentage amongst the three categories for hyphenated names at 16%. I wonder if culture and marital traditions play a big role in the differences between brides’ decisions with their last names across the three ethnicities/races. I also wonder what this data would have looked like a few decades ago and if the results would be significantly different from modern times. This relates to my community because I have witnessed all three options for last names occurring with married women, although taking their spouse’s name seems to be the most common, and it is important to recognize potential deeper meanings behind these choices. My headline for this graph would be: “Keeping vs. Changing Last Names - A Simple Concept with a Greater Meaning”.

comments.raw_comment:
What I notice: 
- A comparative bar chart is presented
- Most brides take their spouse’s last name, but the percentage varies by race.
- White brides do this the most (86%), while Hispanic brides do it the least (60%).
- Black brides are the most likely to hyphenate their names (16%).
What I wonder: 
- Why do Hispanic brides keep their last name more often?
- How do culture and religion influence these choices?
- Would the trend be different in same-sex marriages?
How this relates to me and my community: 
Being part of a Jewish community, taking a spouse’s last name is not just a tradition but an expectation. In many Jewish marriages, women adopt their husband’s surname as part of religious and cultural norms. However, hyphenating last names is pretty common in my community, often to honor both family names and maintain a connection to one’s heritage. However, keeping a maiden name entirely is unheard of, as it may be seen as breaking from tradition.
Catchy headline: "Tying the Knot, Changing the Name?"

I notice that American women taking their spouses' names is the most common choice, which historically speaking has been the case. Black brides were most likely to hyphenate their names (16%) and Hispanic brides were more likely to keep their name (30%).

I wonder why such the different ethnic groups are more likely to keep their spouses name, their own name, or hyphenate. I am speculating it has something to do with culture and tradition, as mentioned previously, the majority of women take their husband's last name because that is what has usually been done in Western Society. I know that Hispanic surnames are really important meaning - wise, especially in such family-centric cultures, so the carrying on of the familial history through the name could be one contributor of Hispanic women keeping their own name. I would assume the same is true for Black women who want to preserve their family history. 

This relates to me and my community because I will likely get married, and am part of the new generation that will marry. As a non-white person of mixed race, I've definitely thought about hyphenating my own name. I think this trend will increase as more people have interracial marriages. 

"Something Old, Something New, or Something Borrowed"

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that American women change their names to varying degrees: 86% of White brides, 73% of Black brides, 60% of Hispanic brides take their spouse's name. Interestingly, Black brides were most likely to hyphenate their names (16%) and Hispanic brides were more likely to keep their name (30%).

I wonder why such a large number of White brides take their spouse's name. Perhaps tradition dictates this trend. Furthermore, since Hispanic individuals often have more than one middle name, perhaps it is related to the bride's not changing their name. I wonder if fewer women will take their spouse's name in the future, considering how difficult it can be to change legal documents.

This relates to me and my community because my generation will be getting married in the next 15 years. As more couples are of mixed race, these statistics may change. I imagine that the number of brides that take their spouse's names will decrease across all races.

"Getting Hitched: Ditching the Name"

comments.raw_comment:
Major Racial differences between last names	

In the website of brides changing their last names, we have noticed similar and different things. The graph is separated into how likely the bride change their last name based on race. The graph shows that white people choose to take the spouse's last name more commonly than Hispanics and black people do. While Hispanics are more likely to keep their last name than both black and white people are. Interestingly, white and Hispanic peoples data add up to 99% while black people’s data add up to 98%. Wondering where the missing percentages are going. We are also left wondering why it’s only those three races and not more. It might show others why some races are most likely to change their last name or keep it. We believe that this information has little impact on ourselves or our community. In conclusion,  we are a little surprised that the difference in brides' likelihood to give up their maiden name varies so much by race.

comments.raw_comment: There are a few trends I notice in the data presented, and I’m interested to know the reasons behind them. Firstly, the demographic most likely to take their husbands names are white brides, while black and hispanic brides are increasingly less likely to take their husband’s names. Black brides were by far the most likely to hyphenate their names, while Hispanic brides were the most likely to keep their maiden names. Of the white brides that did not take their husbands’ names the majority kept their maiden name, rather than hyphenate. I could speculate this to reflect different cultural norms around marriage. Particularly, you could see the significant minority of white brides keeping their maiden names as representing the population of progressive educated professional white women and the 90% who don’t as those who follow more traditional and Christian social moores, which is a division I’ve noticed in my life and communities.

I wonder how different the results would have been if the polling had been opened up to a large pool of sexualities and races. I think those changes would make the results more representative of the women of the United States. This relates to me because my mom did not change her last name and it is interesting to see how much of a minority her choice was. A possible headline would be "To change your name or to keep your name"

comments.raw_comment: This graph depicts the percentage of brides changing their last name, either taking their spouse's name, keeping their name, or hyphenating it. The percentages vary based on race. I notice that most women of all races take their spouse's last names. I think this is simply because of tradition. Although a fairly large percentage of Hispanic women kept their last name, this may suggest that this tradition of taking your spouse's last name is not very important to Hispanic culture. I wonder if their are other gender traditions that Hispanic culture does not follow. I notice that out of all women who hyphenate their last name, Black women make up the majority, even though it is only 16 percent. I wonder if as time passes, and as a society progress, fewer women will take their spouse's name. I additionally wonder if white women will be the last to completely switch, if there ever is a complete switch. This affects me and my community as since I am a girl, if I get married, I will have to make the choice on what my last name will be. "To Keep or to Change?"

Thirty percent of Hispanic brides chose not to change their last name, having the highest percentage of brides who chose not to change it. While black brides chose to Hyphenate their last name with their spouse’s. 

I wonder why black brides choose to get a hyphenated last name. I also wonder how the culture of taking the spouse's last name came about. 
This affects me and my community because as a Hispanic person, I understand why Hispanic brides choose to keep their last names. In Hispanic culture, people tend to have two last names. This is because the first surname of both parents is given to the children in a hyphenated style surname.
What Are Women Choosing To Do WIth Their Last Names After Marriage?

comments.raw_comment: The graph is showcasing brides taking their spouse's last names, keeping their last name, or hyphenating their last name amongst ethnicities such as white, black, and hispanic. Amongst the white brides surveyed white women had the highest percentage of taking their spouse's last name at 86%. I wonder if divorce rates amongst different ethnicities have an effect on whether they take their partner's last name. I also wonder if the length of the relationship before getting married has an effect on whether the bride takes their partner's last name.  As a Hispanic I thought it would have the highest percentage of brides hyphenating their last name. Instead it was 7% less than black brides taking hyphenating their last name with their partners. In the future I believe more brides will begin to just keep their last name or hyphenate them. This is because as people are getting married less and getting married more later in their life they feel more attached to their name. Another reason is because it is becoming more socially acceptable for a bride to keep her last name. Furthermore, I am interested to see how this chart changes in the future, and the reasoning behind it.

This graph depicts the results of a survey that asked 2,740 married women of different races in opposite-sex marriages what they did with their last names after marriage. The researchers focused on women from three ethnic categories: White, Black, and Hispanic. The graph clearly shows that, no matter what ethnic background, the majority of women choose to take their partner's last name. 

 However, out of everyone in the survey,Hispanic women were the  most likely to keep their last name with thirty percent of them keeping their name. In comparison only nine percent of  black women w and  ten percent of white women kept their name. I'm curious if Hispanic women keeping their own names has to do with culture. I'm curious why they didn't broaden this survey to include more cultures, which would provide more information if keeping one last name is a cultural phenomena. This is relevant to my community because all of the married women I know have taken their spouses' names, and when I get married, I intend to do the same.

In this graph, I noticed that a majority of women of every race are more likely to take their husband's last name than to keep their own. 86% of White women, 73% of black women, and 60% of Hispanic women. I noticed that Hispanic women are the most likely to keep their maiden name with 30% of Hispanic women not taking their husband's last name. I wonder how much this percentage has changed in the last 20 years as I feel that the public is more open to women keeping their last names. I think it can be seen as empowering for women to keep their maiden name. Especially for women in the medical and law field who work for years to earn a degree, only to have someone else's last name attached to it.  I wonder why it is tradition for women to take the man's last name and with the women's movement still on the rise if it will become more normalized for a man to take their wife's last name. This relates to me and my community because I am a girl and at some point in time I will have to decide whether or not I will take my husband's last name or keep my own.

I also find it interesting that in general, more women take their spouse's last name than don't. I wonder why this is. I wonder why it became a tradition for women to take their spouse's last name and why White people partake more in this custom than other races. I also wonder why Black people hyphenate their last names more than other races. This relates to myself and my community as most women I know took their spouse's name after marriage. I do not know any married women who kept their last name or hyphenated their last name. I wonder if as time progresses and society becomes less patriarchal women will stop changing their last names and will be proud to keep their names.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph shows the results from a survey that asked 2,740 married women in opposite-sex marriages what they do with their last names after marriage. The researchers separated these women into three categories based on their races (White, Black, and Hispanic). It is clear from this graph that the overwhelming majority of women take their spouse's name throughout all three races. However, out of all the races surveyed, Hispanic women were most likely to keep their last name as 30% of them chose to keep it compared to Black women (9%) and White (10%). While this graph only surveyed a tiny percentage of America's 332 million-person population, I think that Hispanic women's commitment to keeping their last name shows the pride that they have in maintaining their heritage, especially as a race that is so often discriminated against. Black women show similar respect for their heritage as 16% of Black women hyphenated their last names compared to 3% of White women and 9% of Hispanic women. This is interesting because I feel like I have never heard a hyphenated last name. I wonder how this graph would change if more people and races were included. For example, Asian women were left out of this graph as mentioned in the commentary. This relates to me because I am a young woman who hopes to get married one day, and eventually, will have to decide what to do with my last name. 
"Name Norms after Marriage"

comments.raw_comment:
The graph depicts the percentage of brides, based on their race, and their decision to change their name last after matrimony. For example, this graph shows that statistically, the majority of white brides, end up taking their spouse’s last name (86%). While a majority of Hispanic brides still take their spouse’s last name (60%), Hispanic brides are the most likely to keep their maiden names at 30% compared to white brides (10%) and Black brides (9%). What I wonder is why this survey was so limited. I understand this was a voluntary survey and only 2,740 American brides responded. Even though it was conducted by the Pew Research Center, a reliable source, it does not accurately represent women across America 68.45 million married women across America. Plus, this graph only pertains to same-sex couples and does not include Asian or Indigenous people. I wonder how much this graph would fluctuate if more people responded and more groups were represented. This relates to my community because as a young woman surrounded by other young women, if we choose to get married, we all have to one day decide the fate of our last names. More and more women feel less pressure to have to change their name to please their husbands and decaying, misogynistic societal standards. It will be interesting to see who leaves their last name, who keeps their last name, and who hyphenates.  

“Married Women: Who Will Have to Change Their Drivers License?”

comments.raw_comment:
This chart notes the percentage of women changing their last name in marriage across various racial groups.  White women are the most likely to change their last name to that of their husband's. Black women are most likely to hyphenate their last names, and Hispanic women are extremely likely to keep their last name altogether. 
I wonder why Hispanic women keep their name the most among the racial groups polled for the graph. While only 1 in 10 black or white women keep their name, around 1 in 3 Hispanic women do, which is a huge leap. Maybe it's for a cultural reason? I think that Hispanic families tend to be more close-knit, and many Hispanic people live in intergenerational households. It could be for this reason that Hispanic women want to keep this connection to their family and not take their husbands name.
More and more women are choosing to not take the traditional route of taking the husband's last name. It's interesting to see how this trend is occurring among various groups, especially since there are many women in my life.
HEADLINE: I Do or Don't: Say Yes to the Name

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, it is depicting the percentage of bridges who either took their spouse’s last name, kept their last name, or hyphenated the names for three different ethnicities/races (white, black, and hispanic). I noticed that across all three ethnicities/races, the majority of brides took their spouse’s name, with whites having the highest percentage of 86%. Additionally, I noticed that hispanic brides have the highest percentage of keeping their name with a percentage of 30% whereas white and black brides were less likely to keep their names. Also, black brides had the highest percentage amongst the three categories for hyphenated names at 16%. I wonder if culture and marital traditions play a big role in the differences between brides’ decisions with their last names across the three ethnicities/races. I also wonder what this data would have looked like a few decades ago and if the results would be significantly different from modern times. This relates to my community because I have witnessed all three options for last names occurring with married women, although taking their spouse’s name seems to be the most common, and it is important to recognize potential deeper meanings behind these choices. My headline for this graph would be: “Keeping vs. Changing Last Names - A Simple Concept with a Greater Meaning”.

This graph depicts brides in opposite-sex marriages with their partner's last name. There are 3 options shown that depict what opposite-sex people do which are to take a spouse's name, keep their own last name, or hyphenate their last name with their partners. I noticed that the highest percentage of brides who took their husband's last names were white and the highest percentage of people who hyphenated their last names were black. I wonder how race affects this topic in the first place and why it's brought up -- like what does skin color have to do with marriage and taking your partner's last name? I think that the surveyors believe that race and ethnicity play a role due to the culture of that individual which can affect the decisions they make. This relates to my community because I firsthand know many women who have taken their husband's last names for personal life but would hyphenate them for business/job purposes. It depends on the individual and the choice that they make but personally, when the time comes to marry my future man I will take the traditional route and take his last name.

comments.raw_comment:
In the chart, I noticed that White women are most likely to take their spouse's last name with a 86% chance. This includes a 3% chance of White women who hyphenate their maiden and husband’s last name, and only a low 10% who actually keep their maiden name. On the other hand, Hispanic women are least likely to take their spouse's name with a 60% chance, and a 30% chance of keeping their maiden name. While Black women are most likely to hyphenate their last name. I wonder if it is most common for Hispanic women to keep their maiden name because of the importance of family. This may be because with Hispanic tradition, a woman’s last name is kept to carry their father’s last name as an important part of their identity. Also, Hispanic women often keep both their maiden name and add their husband’s last name on. Additionally, why are white women most likely to take their spouse’s name? This relates to my community as last names are a part of a person’s identity. When I get married, I will probably take my spouse’s last name, but I wonder how this will change for my friends. 


“From Miss to Mrs: Ditching or Keeping the Last Name”

I notice that American women change their names to varying degrees: 86% of White brides, 73% of Black brides, 60% of Hispanic brides take their spouse's name. Interestingly, Black brides were most likely to hyphenate their names (16%) and Hispanic brides were more likely to keep their name (30%).

I wonder why such a large number of White brides take their spouse's name. Perhaps tradition dictates this trend. Furthermore, since Hispanic individuals often have more than one middle name, perhaps it is related to the bride's not changing their name. I wonder if fewer women will take their spouse's name in the future, considering how difficult it can be to change legal documents.

This relates to me and my community because my generation will be getting married in the next 15 years. As more couples are of mixed race, these statistics may change. I imagine that the number of brides that take their spouse's names will decrease across all races.

"Getting Hitched: Ditching the Name"

comments.raw_comment:
White brides tend to hold onto their names the least, with 86% choosing to take their spouses names. On the contrary, only 60% of Hispanic brides choose to take their spouse's name, with 30% keeping their surname. Black brides are in the middle, with 73% choosing to take their spouses names. They have the highest percentage (16%) of hyphenated names.

Why do white brides highly tend to take their spouses names while Hispanic brides don’t as much? Is this related to the differences between white and Hispanic cultures? It could possibly be due to gender dynamics between these cultures, though in the modern world these differences have been muted.

This shows the disparity between brides’ decisions to choose their surnames depending on their race. It isn’t of much impact to me, but it may be impactful to people who are dedicated to their surnames (like people who have important generational surnames).
